ai.summary: The Modified Duke Criteria are a standardized diagnostic tool used to evaluate suspected infective endocarditis. They stratify patients into 'Definite', 'Possible', or 'Rejected' categories based on clinical, microbiological, and echocardiographic findings.

b: Definite IE: Pathological or clinical evidence
Possible IE: 1 major and 1 minor, or 3 minor criteria
Rejected: Alternative diagnosis or symptom resolution within 4 days
sections.p: Diagnosis requires a combination of major and minor criteria. A 'Definite' diagnosis is reached with 2 major criteria, 1 major and 3 minor criteria, or 5 minor criteria.
Evidence of typical organisms from blood cultures is a hallmark of endocarditis.

t.b: S. viridans, S. bovis, or HACEK group found in two separate blood cultures
Organisms recovered from cultures drawn >12 hours apart
Single positive culture or IgG antibody titer >1:800

sections.p: Echocardiography identifies structural damage or vegetations on cardiac valves and endocardial surfaces.

t.b: Presence of vegetation, abscess, or new valvular regurgitation

b: Predisposition: Heart condition or IV drug use
Vascular phenomena: Emboli, mycotic aneurysms, or Janeway lesions
Immunological phenomena: Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, or Roth spots
Microbiological evidence: Positive cultures not meeting major criteria
sections.p: These include predisposing factors and systemic manifestations of the infection.

b: Acute Rheumatic Fever: Both present with fever and murmur, but Rheumatic Fever follows a strep throat infection and has specific Jones criteria findings like chorea.
Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE): Can cause Libman-Sacks endocarditis (sterile vegetations) and skin rashes that mimic embolic phenomena.
Atrial Myxoma: A benign heart tumor that can cause systemic emboli and constitutional symptoms similar to IE.
Prior Antibiotic Use: Can result in 'Culture-Negative Endocarditis', making it difficult to satisfy the major microbiological criterion.
Early Disease: Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE) may be negative in up to 30% of cases, especially if vegetations are small (<2mm).
Right-sided Endocarditis: Often seen in IV drug users; peripheral stigmata like Osler nodes are frequently absent because emboli go to the lungs rather than the systemic circulation.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent high fever with night sweats
Small, painful nodules on fingers or toes
Shortness of breath or worsening leg swelling
